statement: A captured enemy agent can be turned and operated as a double agent, transmitting to his original service intelligence that the capturing service has devised and controls.
Run at scale, a double-agent network can move beyond piecemeal deception to actively run and control an adversary's entire espionage apparatus within a country.
A primary objective of running double agents is to control the enemy intelligence system, or as much of it as can be reached.
Use the controlled double-agent network to detect and catch newly arrived enemy spies as they appear.
Exploit captured agents and their contacts to learn the personalities, methods, codes, and cyphers of the enemy secret service.
The questions an enemy service sends its agents reveal its plans and intentions, so the enemy's own questionnaires should be harvested as an intelligence source on what the enemy wants to know.
Influence the enemy's decisions by controlling the answers its agents send back to it.
The highest purpose of controlled double-agent traffic is to deceive the enemy about one's own plans and intentions.
The most profitable double-agent cases are those in which the case officer immerses himself so completely in the agent's persona that he achieves total psychological empathy with him.

It is frequently preferable to keep a known enemy agent under surveillance and control than to arrest him, because eliminating one operation only spurs the enemy to mount another that must then be found afresh.
condition: when the agent can be denied access to genuine intelligence

statement: Neutralise an enemy agent without arrest by cutting him off from genuine intelligence and feeding him low-value true-but-harmless material known as 'chicken feed'.
Turning a captured spy to work for you is the best outcome, because a controlled or neutralised enemy service ceases to be a threat.
Run all double agents as one interrelated system whose cases are kept mutually consistent and in balance, never as isolated operations.

The real test of a deception is the enemy's internal reaction to the planted material, assessed by monitoring the enemy's own communications, not the mere delivery or apparent acceptance of the message.

Constant monitoring of all wireless traffic lets the controller check both what a double agent transmits and the messages sent to him, evaluate the enemy's reception, and detect the arrival of new agents.

To take over a wireless double agent who has died or been removed without the enemy detecting the substitution, the operator must first master the agent's individual sending style: key rhythm, idiosyncrasies, and any prearranged warning signals.
condition: if the agent dies or is otherwise removed

statement: Cooperation between the different departments and services involved is the one essential condition for success in double-cross work.
Sustain the agent's persona consistently across every channel of communication with the enemy: wireless, secret writing, and personal contact in neutral countries.
A double agent's position is far more precarious than an ordinary agent's: a single inconsistency can expose and destroy him.
Neutral countries serve as clearing-grounds where an intelligence service can plant information and make it appear credible to the enemy.
A contemporaneous operational report is more reliable and less liable to become propaganda or self-justification than a history of the same events written years later.

Many kinds of double agent exist: a spy turned under pressure or for self-preservation, a genuine volunteer to the other side, an adventurer who serves either side, a captured or executed agent whose traffic the captors keep transmitting, and the wholly fictitious 'notional' agent who never existed.
Most captured spies are not incorruptible fanatics; a majority will agree to work as double agents under pressure or for simple self-preservation.

Run double agents on a long-term basis: postpone exploitation and deliberately build an agent's reputation with the enemy over months or years so he can later be used with confidence and boldness for a substantial purpose.
Expect to invest true information, effort, and money heavily and early in a double-agent case before any payoff; some cases yield nothing, but none pays off unless you pay in freely first.

A claim to control an enemy agent system is bounded in time and circumstance; here it held only from the fall of France in 1940 to the return of Allied armies to France in 1944, and rested on Britain being physically cut off from the Continent.

Controlling an enemy's agent network depends on controlling the physical entry channels into the territory; only when ingress is narrow enough to exclude or detect unknown agents can you plausibly claim to control the whole system.

Run every agent and every message on the assumption that the enemy may also hold independent, uncontrolled agents who can cross-check your traffic, even when you believe you control them all; premature confidence in total control is dangerous.

Excess caution carries a cost: wrongly assuming the enemy held uncontrolled cross-checking agents wasted opportunities and forced a less bold, less effective deception service than was actually possible.

Do not assume a future operation will enjoy comparable conditions; this success rested on extraordinary and unrepeatable good fortune, and running double agents in a next war will be harder and more hazardous.
Treat evolved control methods as illustrations and guides to conduct, not as fixed principles or invariable rules; circumstances change, so adapt the experience rather than apply it mechanically.
Trust a deception channel only when an independent secret source confirms the enemy received the planted material, believed it, and that competing reports did not override it.

Do not over-invest in a single communication technology or abandon older channels because the newest one seems dominant; the attack-defence contest keeps shifting, so preserve personal contact, secret writing, and wireless as alternatives.

Design deception to be consistent with every enemy collection channel, not just the controlled agents; the enemy also learns from aerial reconnaissance, wireless intercepts, POW interrogation, prior knowledge and the press, and neutral embassies, any of which can expose a false agent report.

Even when you cannot safely feed false information for fear of contradiction by other enemy channels, controlling one of the enemy's main information sources is itself a great gain: you learn exactly what the enemy knows, replacing fear of a possible leak with certainty about whether he holds it.

Denying the enemy all information is the security ideal but is unattainable; a more achievable aim is to control one of his main sources so you can know, select, pervert, and ultimately deceive through it.

Controlling the enemy's supply of agent news is more effective than trying to suppress all his agents, because a service kept adequately supplied has little incentive to build a second, unknown network.

Exploit the enemy's habit of giving each new spy a fallback contact: although espionage doctrine forbids letting one agent know another, new agents are often handed a lifeline that turns out to be one of your already-controlled men, delivering the newcomer to you.
Use detailed knowledge of how your controlled agents were trained, briefed, and equipped as a template to detect and expose other, uncontrolled enemy agents when they appear.

Read the cessation of a line of enemy questioning as intelligence in its own right: when the enemy stops asking about a topic such as beach and ground defences, it signals he has abandoned the related intention such as invasion.
Use controlled-agent answers not only to inform but to shape enemy action, nudging his targeting choices and injecting strategic propaganda through plausibly sourced replies.
A long period of truthful reporting is usually a necessary precondition for passing over a lie; the force of any misinformation depends on the established reputation of the sender.
Build a double agent up gradually and always in line with what the enemy expects or believes he could plausibly obtain; during this novitiate he is a liability, not an asset.
The larger the intended prize from a double agent, the higher the preliminary stake of genuine information that must be paid to build his credibility.

Because a controlled agent cannot ignore a question without destroying his case, some answer is unavoidable; each release therefore requires a case-by-case profit-and-loss assessment made jointly by those who know the agent's potential and those with technical knowledge of the subject.
No message should ever reach the enemy that has not been approved by a competent central authority; a single approval gate for all outgoing traffic is the lifeline of a double-cross system.

The agency that runs double agents must not be the same body that decides what intelligence may be released to the enemy: a service cannot be trusted to give away its own secrets and keep its agents, so release authority must sit with an impartial higher body.
Vest ultimate authority to approve traffic to the enemy at as high a level as possible, because that responsibility is a dangerous power that lower levels cannot properly carry.

Keep the traffic of different agents mutually consistent to avoid glaring contradictions, but ensure their reports do not resemble one another too closely either; both contradiction and suspicious similarity betray control to an enemy comparing agents.

An enemy comparing several agents will distrust those who contradict each other on easily verifiable facts, and will abandon an agent whose reports are contradicted by a more credible source such as air reconnaissance, the press, or POW reports.

Double agents are best run by an impartial counterespionage or security department that has studied the enemy secret service, not by a service department pursuing its own narrow interest; ignorance of enemy personalities and methods causes practical errors, and single-interest control distorts the case.
Keep the counterespionage purpose of double-agent work in the foreground; a body pursuing deception alone is too easily seduced by its dazzling prizes and will spend the agent too soon.

The best agents for high-level deception are long-distance agents carefully built up over a long apprenticeship, and are best produced by running them for counterespionage first; agents developed purely for deception tend to be used prematurely and blown for short-term gain.
Do not sacrifice a long-built double-agent case for an immediate intelligence or penetration bonus; cashing out early can lose a channel of far greater long-term deception value.
No traffic of any kind should be sent to the enemy without the written approval of a competent authority; approval must be documented, not merely verbal.
Use double agents the enemy has already recruited; do not try to manufacture one by throwing your own man in the enemy's path ('coat-trailing'), which almost always fails.
exception: does not apply to wholly notional agents, which are a separate category

statement: An enemy handler's prestige and income are often tied to the reputation of the agents he personally recruited, making him their fiercest defender against doubts from rivals or headquarters; a controlled agent thus gains a built-in protector inside the enemy service.
A zealous case officer tends to become obsessed with the importance and impeccability of his own cases and, even from good motives, resists subordinating them to the general interest.

A double agent should as far as possible actually live the life and go through the motions of a genuine agent: if tasked to report on a place, he or a substitute should really go and observe it, so his messages ring true and survive scrutiny.

Give a cover story real substance: if an agent notionally has a subagent or cut-out, he should actually have one and have met him, because no one can memorise and stay infallible on a lengthy wholly-fictitious tale under interrogation.
Never build a cover on an early lie; ground it in actually-experienced truth, because a false detail cannot be recovered and detailed questioning will eventually expose the discrepancy.
An agent who wants high standing should obey his handler's instructions as nearly as possible and not switch his declared line of interest, or his reports lose weight.

Retain the initiative: within his instructions, use the agent to provoke the enemy into asking the questions you are prepared to answer rather than those you must avoid, because a passive, defensive posture eventually leads to trouble or the collapse of the case.

Position agents far in advance through their notional business or private life so they are plausibly placed at the crucial moment; because plans cannot be fixed long ahead, control must anticipate events and stay several moves ahead, guessing the future and hoping to guess right more often than wrong.

Assign one dedicated case officer to each case who knows every detail and runs it day to day; this is essential for wireless agents who must answer quickly and for judging the relevance of each enemy question against the case history.

Set case policy at the section level, not by the case officer alone, because what is best for a single case is not always best for the system as a whole and sacrifices in the general interest must sometimes override a case officer's wishes.
Do not overburden a case officer: no officer should handle more than two major cases at once, and ideally only one, or cases will be neglected at critical moments and may be irretrievably ruined.
Make a careful psychological study of each agent and keep him under watch, because a coerced agent may later feel remorse, refuse to continue, or turn against you unexpectedly.

Gradually converting a coerced agent into a willing collaborator is well worth the effort: an agent who takes genuine interest offers useful suggestions and is worth far more than one working under compulsion.
Study every idiosyncrasy of a willing agent and satisfy even his extravagant demands as far as possible, or he will not give the fullest and most useful service of which he is capable.

Keep every double agent busy, ideally with an actual job apart from espionage, because such agents are prone to vanity, moodiness, and introspection, and idleness breeds the brooding that endangers a case.

Make a fixed and generous financial agreement with each agent as early as possible, and let voluntary agents share a percentage of the money the enemy pays, since the incentive stimulates effort and better suggestions.

Establish from the outset that all money the enemy sends belongs in right and in fact to the controlling service, and that the agent's percentage is a reward for collaboration rather than his own earnings.
The sum an enemy service pays an agent is a rough but generally reliable indicator of the trust it places in him.
Act decisively and rapidly at the start of a case, even at considerable risk, because the enemy will not credit an agent who delays making contact without a reasonable explanation.

Before transmitting, assume a captured agent is withholding part of his story and possibly a concealed warning or distress signal until he trusts you more than the enemy; surface his full history first or his early messages may betray him.

Balance the competing needs of a quick start and a complete prior debrief; in practice start once the main lines of the agent's story are fairly certain, and meanwhile alter his messages in nonessentials such as dating, word order, and word choice to defeat any undisclosed warning signal.

Obtain a detailed life-history of the agent from his earliest years, because any deviation from truth will eventually be detected, the more detail an agent gives the more certainly he trips himself if he lies, and deep knowledge of his past prevents inconsistencies in his messages.

For a wireless agent, determine whether the enemy recorded his sending style during training: if so he must key his own messages, and in any case let the agent construct his own messages, since stylistic idiosyncrasies are easily recognised but not easily reproduced.
When you must start a wireless case before fully investigating the agent, get one message across and then simulate a transmitter breakdown to buy time for further research into his history.
Double agents recruited in the field or in newly liberated territory are harder to run successfully, because a quick start cannot be reconciled with the need for a complete prior debrief.

Keep a careful, minute, and continuous record of every case, comprising the actual enemy traffic plus a log of the agent's conversations, journeys, and actions, because counterespionage succeeds through patient study of records and only a well-kept record prevents the eventual blunder or inconsistency that blows an agent.
Controlled agents' morale and bomb-damage reporting can serve as a weapon of political warfare, so coordinate with a political-warfare body to exploit the reports' effect on enemy leadership.
condition: when the enemy service is trusted by its own high command

statement: Keep case records focused and prune them periodically; over-elaborate files bury a case's essential features under redundant detail and make it hard to be sure nothing important has been overlooked.

Keep every agent clear and independent of other agents, so that if one is blown he does not bring down the others and a single agent can be risked without endangering the rest; permit a linkage between agents only when it cannot be avoided.
exception: a minimal appeal or emergency-funds contact between two agents is sometimes unavoidable without creating suspicion

statement: A discrepancy that looks damning from your complete records is unlikely to be caught by the enemy, because his handler forwards reports to higher authority uncritically and that authority lacks the detailed case knowledge to spot the contradiction.

A well-established agent is extremely hard to blow: when a deception is later exposed the enemy usually prefers more credible explanations, that his honest agent was misled, that the plan was abandoned, or that he was himself deceived by the cover, over the truth that he was a double cross for years.
Once an agent is trusted, even blatant gaffes will not easily convince the enemy that he is controlled; established trust is sticky and resists contrary evidence.

Never commit an irrevocable act in running a double agent if it can be avoided, because you cannot predict the future; refraining almost always proves right, and a case left intact tends to revive, often in an unexpected way.

Do not overestimate the enemy's ability to correlate and detect a suspect agent; he works with uncertain, imperfectly integrated data, and his officer may be reposted, his records destroyed, or he and his staff simply inefficient.

Holding a doubtful case rather than acting on it demands patience, confidence, and a willingness to face the charge of lacking initiative, yet inaction at a doubtful moment almost invariably proves right.
When suitable agents are numerous, favour quality over quantity; too many cases overload the limited case officers and dilute the practical effect of each one.

A well-connected agent who can only relay high-level gossip or embassy rumour is not high-grade, because indiscreet ministerial or diplomatic talk carries little conviction; the enemy staff needs verifiable facts on which to base its appreciations.

The most valuable agent is often a lowly placed one: a seaman or wireless operator can supply far more useful factual intelligence on convoys or unit movements than a well-connected spy of the traditional pattern.

Grade a double agent on two axes, whether the enemy genuinely trusts him and whether he is plausibly positioned to supply facts even in a narrow field, and establish a high-quality agent firmly on both.

For pure deception a notional wholly fictitious agent can be preferable to a real one, since it can be controlled and placed at will without the risks and limits of a live man, whereas for most other purposes the agent who keeps nearest to the truth is best.
Counterespionage must be a continuous process that persists in peace as well as war, because you can never be certain against whom it will need to be directed in a few years' time.
Treat any power that engages in espionage as a legitimate target for counterespionage measures, whether that power is for the moment friend or foe.
No counterespionage service can prevent all espionage, but a good one can keep its controlling finger on all espionage and be ready to strike at it at any moment.

A carefully cultivated double-agent system is the safest and surest weapon of counterespionage and the most adaptable to changing conditions, problems, and even changing enemies, because controlling the enemy's own agents yields knowledge of his methods, intentions, and personnel.
Intercepting mail to and from known enemy cover addresses exposes agents in secret contact with the enemy.
When you detect a suspected agent in contact with the enemy, holding off arrest in anticipation of a voluntary confession can yield a turning opportunity rather than mere neutralisation.
A single turned agent, worked patiently, can expose several other enemy agents, their paymasters, and their sabotage plans early enough to prepare countermeasures.
Running a double agent's wireless link yields the enemy's codes and cypher procedures, which can in turn help break other enemy traffic.
A skilled wireless interceptor can identify an enemy transmitting station by its note and each operator by his individual sending style.
Controlled agents run in parallel under strict compartmentation often deduce one another's true status over time, so compartmentation degrades and cannot be assumed permanent.

When two of your controlled agents are kept unaware of each other's true allegiance, their mutual misreading can escalate dangerously and nearly blow both; manage what each controlled man is allowed to believe about the other.
Exploit plausible external circumstances such as weather or chance to explain away an operational failure to the enemy and preserve the agent's standing.
A controlled channel gives advance warning of incoming enemy agents, revealing who is being sent, when, and where they will arrive.
Poorly trained and equipped infiltrators are easily caught and often cannot even establish wireless contact with their own service without assistance, from lack of technical skill or defective sets.
Use knowledge of how the enemy forges identity documents, gained from a controlled agent, to detect newly arrived agents carrying the same fabricated papers.
The money and equipment an enemy gives an agent signal his expected role and duration, for example a small sum indicating a short pre-invasion mission.

To turn an infiltrator into a double agent, capture him immediately after landing and keep the capture secret, because delay lets him make his own contact with the enemy and any publicity lets the enemy deduce he was caught.
Turn a captured spy by convincing him he can save his life by working for you.
Before running a turned wireless agent, satisfy yourself that his code is fully understood and that messages can be sent which convince the enemy he is genuinely at work.
Never relax vigilance on a converted agent out of premature confidence; a single lapse in supervision can let him escape or turn and wreck the whole system.
A converted agent left without close psychological supervision will eventually destroy his own case in a mood of despair or in a belated effort to restore his self-esteem.
Induce a captured agent to give up his associates by promising leniency for them, such as sparing the life of the follower he expects.
Keep a captured spy alive even if he cannot transmit, since a live spy remains useful as a reference source while a dead spy is of no use.

Execute a calculated few captured agents, both to satisfy public opinion that security is maintained and to convince the enemy that his surviving agents are genuinely free and uncontrolled, because it strains credulity that all of his agents survived their landings.
Scrutinise an agent's identity and travel documents as a primary detection tool, because forged papers routinely carry gross technical errors that betray the enemy's agents.
A double-agent case starves and dies without a steady supply of good feed material and a clear policy on what to send; a case acquired before you can nourish it is wasted.

The ideal high-value agent has plausible social access across strata, is sponsored or vouched for inside the enemy service, and holds a business cover that justifies frequent travel to neutral meeting grounds.

You cannot close an uncontrollable exfiltration channel such as the diplomatic bag, so seed it with your own dictated material rather than let genuine reporting flow, converting the leak into a deception channel.
Exploit well-placed neutrals as couriers and channels, piggybacking controlled reporting in secret writing on a neutral's legitimate outgoing traffic.

Confirm that you control an entire enemy network gradually, by accumulating evidence from secret sources and cross-references between agents, such as the enemy routing payments or emergency lifelines through your controlled men or one agent naming another as the enemy's best.
A man with genuine pre-existing enemy contact can sometimes be steered back into enemy service on your own initiative, the one form of near-coat-trailing that can succeed.
condition: only when a real prior enemy connection already exists

statement: Do not fragment double-agent control across agencies by arbitrary jurisdiction such as offshore versus onshore or foreign versus domestic; an agent crosses these boundaries, so unify control or place it under a common chief.
Confine knowledge of a double-cross system to the smallest possible circle, and keep it out of the hands of higher authorities who will not use it boldly.

Structure double-agent governance in two tiers: a senior board holding ultimate approval authority, and a weekly working-level inter-departmental committee acting as clearing-house, approving authority, and liaison so departments do not cross each other's lines.
Include a civil or political approving authority alongside the military ones, because civilian departments' interests and information are inevitably involved in the traffic.

A governance body succeeds when its members subordinate their own department's interest to the common goal, more than because its charter is clean; good people make an imperfect structure work, and decisions are best reached by discussion rather than votes.
Make the decision to sacrifice or execute agents deliberately, through a dedicated review body working from the case knowledge of the section head, not ad hoc.

Staff a double-agent section with distinct roles: a small directorate for policy and accept-or-reject decisions, dedicated case officers for the agents' lives and traffic, a technical wireless officer, records and analysis officers, and an officer to collect the intelligence arising from the cases.
An organisation running many agents is far more prone than a lone spy to a consistency blunder that destroys an agent's credit, so rigorous indexing and instantly retrievable records are essential.

Remember that obtaining feed material is only half the task; every item must pass an approving authority, much of a collected report is typically disallowed, and the remainder must be plausibly concocted and also approved.
A message must fit the agent's established pattern of traffic; omit even valuable information that does not fit his usual run, or it betrays him.

Split a deception across several agents so it reaches the enemy in parts rather than resting on a single agent's authority; this is safer and more convincing, but requires careful comparison and dovetailing between the agents.
Keep the circle of those witting of the operation as small as humanly possible, accepting that running double agents requires deceiving people on your own side as well as the enemy.
Operate through cover premises for interviewing newcomers, and avoid collecting feed material in a way that reveals to the source what is being done with it.
Sell a long-term deception capability to stakeholders through the promise of a decisive future payoff, which sustains their support better than incremental day-to-day gains.
In managing a deception channel, what you deny and suppress to the enemy matters at least as much as what you send.

Profile each enemy out-station by the pattern of its questions; each station has characteristic interests and its agents resemble one another, letting you attribute tasking and anticipate what the enemy seeks.
Track the changing pattern of enemy questions over time; a shift in what the enemy asks about reveals a shift in his strategy and intentions.
An enemy instructing his agents to lie low and avoid risks signals that he has no imminent offensive planned and is preserving them for a future operation.
Interpret ambiguous enemy tasking against several competing hypotheses and weigh which is most consistent with all the evidence, rather than leaping to a single reading.
The concentration and unusual specificity of an enemy's questions on one target reveals it as a priority objective and potentially his first point of attack.
Once an agent is firmly established, treat any questionnaire he receives as high-grade intelligence, since it carries far greater and more immediate value than is usually attributed to it.
Do not let mistrust of your own judgment stop you from flagging a significant deduction to those who need it; risk a snub rather than withhold a warning.

Large-scale deception fails without coordinated top-level direction of the desired strategic effect; local operators can execute a deception well but cannot originate strategic goals they are never told.

You cannot stop an enemy attack, but you can channel it: plant material steering his effort toward a target where it does least harm or can be best received, since he will strike somewhere regardless.
Plant deception as apparently stolen or captured documents, which the enemy tends to weigh more heavily than an agent's ordinary reports.
Consider planting a wireless set and codes on the enemy to induce him to play it back under his own control, so you can study his deception technique and turn the double-cross tables.
Use controlled traffic to sow internal friction and distrust within the enemy hierarchy, for example by implying that his own officials are disloyal or plotting.
A financial deception can simultaneously fund your operation, raise an agent's standing with the enemy, and confirm the extent of your control.

Engineer arrangements that make enemy handlers personally benefit, in money or prestige, from your agent, because officials who profit from an agent will defend him against suspicion from their own headquarters.
Enemy officials often wilfully ignore suspicions about their own agents, preferring corrupt or disloyal agents to none at all, because their standing depends on having agents.
Build a strategic threat picture from many small, unrelated, mutually corroborating reports rather than one explicit claim, because indirect corroboration is more convincing.
A deception carried by agents alone fails unless it is backed by corroborating physical reality that the enemy's other channels can confirm, such as actual troop movements.

The essence of counterespionage is prevention, and its greatest successes are invisible, the things that never happened; measure success partly by the absence of enemy activity and read the enemy's non-response as intelligence.

Stage a controlled act of sabotage through an agent to reestablish his standing with the enemy, secure his payment, learn the enemy's other sabotage plans, and obtain samples of his latest sabotage equipment.

Staging a controlled sabotage or physical deception is far harder than it sounds, because to convince the enemy the event must generate genuine press coverage, so you must deceive your own media too, making the incident real enough to be reported yet controlled enough to cause no serious harm.

Maintain a balanced bench of trained, trusted agents in constant readiness for a decisive occasion whose timing you cannot know, refreshing the roster so a ready team always exists at the crucial moment.
Recruit the amateur who, on his own initiative, uncovers your operation or the enemy's; turn the poacher into a gamekeeper.
Use a trusted agent's journey to the enemy to verify another agent's standing, map the enemy's local network, and attempt deeper penetration of the enemy service.

Wind down a doubtful or compromised case safely by feeding the enemy the minimum of exact information and closing it with a plausible, non-alarming reason such as the agent's illness, rather than an abrupt silence.
Do not smooth away every hitch; real-world friction and difficulties in an operation increase the enemy's belief, because a genuine agent would face the same obstacles.

Deliberately constrain an agent's notional circumstances so he has a plausible reason to be unable to answer awkward or dangerous questions; too much freedom, money, or access removes his excuse for not knowing.
Position an agent near a prospective source with an eye to future access, before the access is needed.

Keep a trained substitute able to imitate an agent's sending style so the channel survives his illness, removal, or loss of trust, and separate message-drafting from key-operation once an agent's reliability becomes doubtful.
Split inbound and outbound communication across different channels, for example receiving by wireless and replying by secret writing, for greater security.
When the enemy holds a hostage over an agent, such as his family, you cannot risk sending obvious misinformation through him that would endanger the hostage if the deception were exposed.
Use a controlled agent to exaggerate the strength of your defences and instil a wholesome fear that deters the enemy from acting.
Drop or limit an otherwise-ideal agent whose tasking demands something you cannot safely supply, such as genuine weather data useful to the enemy.

A deception directive is self-defeating if it demands the agent report things a genuine spy in his position would never report, such as good civilian morale; deception must respect what the agent's role would plausibly produce.

The price in genuine information you must pay to keep a channel alive can become too high to justify; weigh that cost against the channel's value, and consider deliberately closing it to force the enemy to rebuild from scratch.
Give the enemy advance information of your defensive measures before you actually implement them, to deter him from attacking.
You cannot pass effective misinformation without knowing what must be concealed and having a consistent plan to support; a channel with no known real plan behind it can only play safe.
An approval body focused only on vetoing risk degrades into pure censorship and wastes the capability; it must also actively enable the mission.
Even a correct vision of future events tends to antedate results; resist premature action that could wreck a capability being built for a later decisive moment.

In a defensive phase the chief value of a controlled channel is concealment; the great deception gains come only in the offensive phase, so spend the defensive phase building the agents' credibility for later use.
Establish a single powerful centralised deception authority, fully informed of both all operational plans and all available deception channels; without it, deception is spasmodic and ineffective.
Keep the organisation that owns the deception channels separate from the operational body that would spend agents for short-term gains, because the channels' value is their long-term credibility.

Everyone who must judge a controlled agent's reliability needs access to the secret feedback sources that reveal whether the enemy believes him; withholding that evidence from decision-makers makes their judgments unreal.
A deception controller who is not told what channels are actually available to him is crippled; the deception director must know his instruments.
A deception capability built gradually through experiment yields better real knowledge of what its channels can and cannot do than one imposed fully formed from the start.
Do not subordinate a double-agent system wholly to deception; it serves counterespionage and intelligence too, so its owner should run the agents while the deception director merely uses the channel.
The deepest triumph of a deception is security, that the real plan is never disclosed or guessed, more than that the cover story is believed.
A deception often succeeds because the enemy deceives himself; design it to reinforce his existing preconceptions and expectations rather than to overcome them.
The surest contribution to a deception is denial of the dangerous truth, not the planting of a lie; and a cover story should stay as near the real thing as safely possible.
An agent is safe reporting a cover story when even the real participants are deceived; keep agents to facts and let them hedge opinions so a later reversal does not expose them.
Once the enemy learns you use cover plans, he demands more detailed and factual verification, raising the bar for future deception.
Never announce a deception baldly; embed within a large flow of genuine reporting the facts from which the enemy will himself deduce the conclusion you want.
Since a controlled agent must answer questions rather than volunteer information, steer the enemy's future questions in the direction you want through the answers you give.

Coordinate counterespionage arrests with deception, because another authority's decision to roll up an enemy network can destroy your best double-agent channel and endanger the agents connected to it.
Fiction suitably presented is often more readily believed than the truth; a well-crafted invented report can outperform a real one.
Report what the enemy expects to hear; confirming his expectations builds his belief faster than surprising him.
Retire a notional subagent who is positioned to observe something you must not report by giving him a plausible illness or death, backed by real corroboration such as a planted obituary.
Structure a notional network so subagents may report outward but all receive their tasking through the controlled head, keeping central control.
If a turned agent's messages consistently draw no enemy response, suspect he has covertly signalled the enemy that he is under control.
A channel that runs through a cooperating insider of the enemy service is the highest-value channel, because you can be sure your information reaches its target and is likely to be believed.
A promising case fails to pay off when it is shared with too many interested departments, its agent's motives are left unresolved, or it is starved of early build-up.

An agent you cannot fully control, such as a seaman meeting the enemy in person, is a liability, because he may divulge what you need suppressed and may fail to convey your misinformation accurately, doing as much harm as good.
An agent whose primary loyalty is to his own cause rather than to you is a weak point, however well equipped and trained.
Secret sources can reveal almost everything about an incoming agent except the one thing that matters most, his true loyalty, which must be judged from his behaviour on arrival.

Before letting a double agent return to enemy territory, ensure he does not know the knowledge you hold through secret sources, since he may be coerced or persuaded into betraying your association; compartmentalise your best intelligence from agents who will re-enter enemy hands.
When the enemy expects your bureaucracy to be slow, defeat that expectation with speed to preserve an agent's credibility.

Capturing the enemy's own intelligence assessment reveals exactly what he knows and which gaps he is trying to fill, showing you precisely where he can be deceived; his questions likewise expose the gaps in his knowledge.
Exaggerate your military strength only within a disciplined bound, on the order of ten percent, enough to mislead or deter but not so much as to strain credulity.
A notional agent can absorb great enemy effort by inventing phantoms, such as a fictitious convoy the enemy prepares to intercept or a non-existent weapon he repeatedly investigates.
Fund a controlled operation through a plausible commercial currency-exchange, so the enemy's foreign payments are converted into your own currency without exposing the arrangement.
A controlled act of sabotage must leave surviving evidence that points to sabotage; too effective an explosion destroys the very clues and planted evidence the enemy needs to credit it.
After a staged incident, plant further clues and steer local investigation and opinion toward the intended explanation so that the press reports it as you wish.
No deception or bluff can be maintained indefinitely; a blunder or sheer mischance will eventually expose it, so there is only a limited window in which to exploit it.
Treat the collapse of one important controlled case as a threat to the whole system, because once the enemy understands your procedure in one case he will re-examine and doubt the rest.
The hardest and most valuable work is often the unglamorous maintenance of a capability intact and ready for its decisive moment, not the flashy operations.

A cover plan cannot be built until the real plan is shared in outline with the deceivers, and it must then continuously track every change in the real plan; deception is downstream of and dependent on operational planning.
The channel-holder must retain a veto over any deception task that would not be believed or would blow the agent, even under pressure, to preserve the channel for the decisive moment.

Use strategic deception to pin enemy forces in place by threatening many landings, preventing their transfer to a decisive front, and design a feint to provoke the enemy into a costly reaction on your own terms.
Fake the appearance the enemy's collection will actually see, such as staging a notional explosion with camouflage for aerial reconnaissance, rather than always mounting a real one.
The enemy recycles captured equipment, so material he supplies to your agents may be your own side's captured kit.
A controlled sabotage yields a domestic security benefit as well, since the resulting publicity stimulates vigilance in real installations.
A returned double agent may take initiatives you cannot foresee or control, even genuinely aiding the enemy; his true loyalty once back in enemy hands is never certain.

A planted deception carried by a corpse or courier must be built around an exhaustively documented personality, with real personal letters, tickets, and identity papers, because the documents are believed only if the man is believed.

Convey the key deception through an informal, personal, off-the-record letter between senior figures rather than an official document, because a candid private letter is more credible and less suspicious.
Draw attention away from your real target by naming it, within the deception, as the enemy's expected cover target, a double-bluff that turns his own suspicion against the truth.
Choose a planting site where the enemy has good access but a thorough forensic examination is difficult, and build in redundant discovery paths so the material is found even by a careless finder.
Choreograph your recovery efforts to escalate gradually and appear not frightened while making it plain you are, so the enemy infers the material is genuinely important without suspecting a plant.
Anticipate that a thorough enemy will consider whether planted material is a deception, so it must withstand scrutiny at the level of every phrase and every corroborating detail.

A triple-cross agent openly declares one controlled channel to you while the enemy believes he keeps a separate hidden channel; run both the declared-controlled and the notionally-uncontrolled traffic to deepen the enemy's confidence.
Offer the enemy a channel he wants to exploit, such as an escape or infiltration route, that you in fact control, so his agents delivered through it are caught while your own assets are inserted.
A strong agent can defuse enemy suspicion in personal contact by shifting the blame for poor results onto the enemy's own failures, such as inadequate funding.
An agent whose primary loyalty is to a third party, such as his own nation or service, forces you to bring that party into the secret, creating a leakage risk you cannot fully control.

Being sure of your own agent's loyalty is not enough; judge also whether the enemy genuinely trusts him or is anticipating his reversion, because an agent the enemy expects to turn back can be used against you.
Political constraints from your own side can stop you developing a case in the way the enemy expects, limiting its value and even threatening its plausibility.
Do not prejudge the ceiling of a case run cautiously under constraints; an exceptionally well-placed agent can become your most valuable even after a limited, guarded start.
Measure the enemy's trust by the sensitivity of what he shares with an agent; handing an agent the enemy's own current cypher is proof of deep trust and a windfall for breaking his other traffic.

One real agent can run an entire notional network of many trusted subagents and contacts, giving vast reporting reach at no real-agent risk; equip him with a notional deputy and substitute operator for continuity.
Give even a notional supporting player his own plausible cover motive, so the network's internal logic holds up under scrutiny.
Remove from the firing line an agent asked questions so high-grade that you cannot supply safe yet plausible answers, because he can no longer sustain his case.
A case dies when the enemy stops paying the agent; withdrawal of payment signals waning enemy interest and starves the channel.
A capability that looks strongest can be closest to failure; do not mistake apparent scale and strength for security.
Build a controlled-agent capability toward a single decisive deception, accepting that the whole network may be spent in that one coup for a payoff that repays years of effort.

When you cannot hide that an operation is coming, deception must instead shift the enemy's belief about its timing and its precise location, and be sustained after the event by suggesting the real blow was only a first move preceding a larger one.
Deception works only within the narrow limits left by the visible reality; you can bend the enemy's belief only so far from what his other channels can plainly see.

Feed the enemy staff the concrete facts, such as unit locations, identifications, headquarters, and assembly areas, from which they will build the false picture themselves, because they trust their own deductions from facts far more than assertions, speculation, or apparent leaks; this is the method of the false order of battle.

Deliver a strategic deception through multiple mutually reinforcing channels, agents plus bogus wireless traffic, visual dummies, real troop movements, and physical regulations, each corroborating the others, because no single channel can carry it.

For the decisive deception, restrict definite deception material to your most-trusted channels while keeping lesser agents running for corroboration and confusion, because even the most trusted channel can collapse unexpectedly and no operation should rest on one.
A deception channel the enemy does not believe is worse than useless, because his reading it in reverse can expose the very truth you meant to conceal.

Continuously assess how far the enemy trusts each agent, using the questions asked, the payments made, remarks in personal contact, and secret intelligence, because an agent's standing oscillates and you must know it before relying on him for a critical task.

A secret shared among many people will inevitably leak given enough time; the growth of an operation multiplies its exposure, and if the enemy learns the scale of your double-cross system he will suspect every agent.
A retreating enemy leaves stay-behind agents, so prepare in advance trained officers ready to capture and turn them the moment territory is retaken.
Enemy agents interned together will develop covert communication and can carry compromising knowledge out on repatriation, so segregate them and control their release.

An uncontrolled freelance fabricator on the enemy's side gravely threatens your deception, because his invented reports compete with yours and may by chance hit the truth; you cannot control what you do not run.

A reorganisation of the enemy service threatens you, because you have learned to exploit its specific personalities, habits, and complacency, and new leadership may sweep away the arrangements you depend on.

An enemy insider defecting to your side can inadvertently destroy your double-agent system, because he will name your controlled agents as the enemy's agents, and the enemy, expecting their arrest, will deduce their control if they keep operating.

Do not place a critical deception's security in an asset who lives in enemy-controlled territory and could be seized or coerced, however loyal; his position to betray you is the risk, independent of his intentions, and do not rely on his own judgment of his safety.

When a linked asset could collapse a deception midway, consider terminating the compromised case at once and even withholding your best channel from the operation, to firewall the rest of the network.

The object of order-of-battle deception is to create in the enemy's mind a belief in the existence and location of notional forces, so that his own logical deduction leads him to the wrong conclusion.

The most valuable moment for a deception can be after the real event; sustain the fiction that the real blow was only a diversion and the main assault is still to come, to keep enemy reserves pinned away from the actual battle.

Seed a deception with verifiable true reports that events will later confirm, such as real units the enemy can check against prisoners, so that when the checkable parts prove accurate he extends his belief to the unverifiable notional parts.
The absence of enemy questions on a topic proves his ignorance of it, and guaranteeing that ignorance by denial contributes as much to an operation's success as any misinformation.

Reinforce a deception from an oblique, non-military angle, such as a plausible commercial or administrative activity implying interest in an area, so the enemy infers the threat from a source unconnected with troop movements.
Use an agent's plausible social access to obtain and pass the corroborating logistical detail, such as rail movement schedules, that makes a notional force concentration credible.
Have an agent credibly report the absence of activity where the real operation is actually staging, confirming the enemy's false expectation of where the blow will fall.
A false but specific, high-confidence warning delivered through a pre-arranged enemy code can pin an enemy reserve away from the real battle for a critical period.
The enemy reusing a code or method with an agent long afterwards is evidence he remains satisfied with that agent; reuse is a trust signal.
The value of a controlled-channel network is measured by its reliability as a safe, efficient instrument that a deception planner can use, not by the plans it carries.

Do not prematurely dissolve a proven capability on a wave of optimism when its main task is done; future uses cannot be forecast, but experience shows a useful weapon will be needed again, probably in an unforeseen way.
Information from sources further back from the front, in the rear or home base, tends to be more reliable and valuable than forward tactical sources.
A veteran, long-established agent carries far more enemy confidence than a new one; newly acquired agents are fit only for short-term tactical use, not long-term strategic build-up.

As a capability's primary advantage recedes, its other uses revive; a multi-purpose controlled-agent system stays valuable because its counterespionage, intelligence, and deception uses rotate over time.

In newly liberated territory a stay-behind enemy agent is very hard to hide and easy to catch amid spy-fever and denunciations, and many will offer to turn; exploit the chaos of liberation to roll up and recruit stay-behind networks.
Replicate a proven governance model, such as an approving committee, for each new theatre rather than forcing local tactical traffic through one distant central body.
A well-executed deception need not blow the agents who carry it; if events confirm their reports they can emerge more trusted than before.
The amount of training and resources the enemy invests in an agent is evidence of his standing; heavy investment signals genuine enemy belief in him.
Do not abandon a case too impatiently for lack of an immediate enemy response, because the enemy may call the agent later.
Sustain a wireless impersonation across operator changes by having each successor copy the predecessor's style, and cover any resulting change in the sending fist with a plausible injury story.

Recognise that the enemy binds his agents with psychological skill, feeding their vanity through mess membership, personal attention, and decorations; use the same techniques on your own agents and expect them on turned ones.
An agent who talks indiscreetly about his secret work is a liability who must be terminated regardless of his other value.

An enemy handler can become so invested in your agent's welfare that he will manage his own superiors to reward and protect the agent, even securing him an enemy decoration; this deep investment is the strongest guarantor of the case and the surest proof of the enemy's belief.
Where complete security against espionage is impossible, such as a facility with large daily access, penetrate the enemy's espionage effort with double agents instead of trying to seal it.
Reposition and extend a controlled network toward future contingencies, a different enemy or postwar counterespionage, to preserve a ready instrument beyond its original purpose.
The enemy's questions can reveal his awareness of and priorities in strategic or emerging technologies, such as atomic research, a high-value intelligence indicator.

Systematically analyse the full body of an enemy's questions and tasking over time; the aggregate yields an accurate picture of his interests and intentions and should be treated as a strategic intelligence product, not merely message by message.
Infer the enemy's true intentions from how he protects his own valuable assets; if he does not warn or move an agent away from a target area, he likely has no imminent devastating plan for it.

When you must report on something the enemy can verify, keep the report substantially accurate but shade the details you control, minimising damage, blurring the precise pattern, and suppressing the actionable specifics.
When the enemy depends on your side for the feedback he needs to correct a weapon or plan, deliberately mis-calibrate that feedback to degrade his effectiveness.
Report truthfully whatever the enemy will learn anyway from other sources, and practise deception only in the margins you actually control.

Shift an enemy's aim by selectively over-reporting overshoots and suppressing undershoots, or the reverse, biasing his correction in the direction that moves his mean point of impact away from the vital target.

When the enemy can cross-check one attribute of an event, such as its timing, give a real event but pair it with a falsified attribute he will use for his correction, for example a real impact reported with the timestamp of a shorter-falling shot.
When an uncontrolled source is also feeding the enemy, model its effect and counter-bias your own reporting to bring the enemy's aggregate picture to where you want it.

Use your most isolated, least-connected, and most-expendable agents for the riskiest deceptions, because their collapse will not bring down the network; keep valuable and linked agents away from high-risk lies.
A deception confined to a single domain, such as naval or technical matters, can be run by one authority without the broad coordination a joint military deception requires.
Protect a real capability through long-term deception that misstates its operating principle and minimises its efficiency, denying the enemy the knowledge he needs to counter it.
Build a notional source's credibility by feeding through him advance true information the enemy cannot yet have and will later independently confirm; verifiable scoops raise a source's standing.
A notional threat, such as fictitious minefields, can deny the enemy large operating areas, especially when a chance real event appears to corroborate it.
To make an agent serve you well, attend to his personal wishes and private interests; caring for his mundane personal concerns binds him.

A running double-cross operator must constantly ask the mirror question, whether the enemy is turning the same weapon against him; never let apparent success persuade you that you are not also being deceived, and do not attribute success to superior cleverness, since the adversary may be your equal in tradecraft.

Absolute personal integrity and the exclusion of all personal considerations, profit, prestige, or self-interest, among every officer is the first and fundamental condition of success in secret intelligence work; corrupt self-interest destroys honest judgment and is the root of most failures, and is the flaw to exploit in the adversary.

In wartime the dice are loaded against the spy, so espionage in the enemy's home country is difficult and usually unprofitable while counterespionage is comparatively easy and yields the richest returns; in peacetime the reverse holds.
A straight agent can succeed in enemy-occupied country, aided by resistance movements or popular goodwill, but his case is almost hopeless in the enemy's own home country.

Unify the espionage and counterespionage services as closely as possible, or at least give each fully accessible records of the other, because they deal with the same problems and the same persons and division causes failure.
